target: AG1’s initial claim that AI is good for society because it improves convenience, health, productivity, accessibility, and workplace safety.
objection: AI harms the economic well-being of many people and businesses by automating/displacing tasks and concentrating gains rather than broadly sharing benefits; it also undermines critical thinking, worsens racial fairness by reproducing bias, and poses serious privacy risks, so these harms can outweigh the claimed benefits.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably creates dangerous privacy harms.
objection: AI privacy and security harms are not unavoidable, because privacy-preserving deployment practices such as data minimization, access controls, encryption, and other safeguards can substantially reduce sensitive-data exposure.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably worsens racial-minority outcomes through discrimination.
objection: AI discriminatory outcomes are not inevitable, because fairness testing, auditing, better data curation, and bias-mitigation techniques can identify and reduce disparate impacts.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily causes net economic harm through automation.
objection: Economic harm from automation is not fixed, because AI can raise productivity and create new tasks and roles, and any displacement can be mitigated through retraining and labor-transition policies.

target: AG2’s claim that AI use in education weakens critical thinking.
objection: AI used in education can support rather than replace reasoning—for example through step-by-step tutoring, explanations, and interactive feedback that requires the learner to generate and evaluate their own answers.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can improve workplace safety and therefore social well-being.
objection: AI can reduce workplace hazards, but AG2’s main rebuttal at this stage is that overall social welfare cannot be assessed by safety benefits alone because other major harms still matter; the safety benefit does not by itself establish that AI is good for society overall.

target: AG1’s claim that AI can help marginalized groups by improving accessibility for people with disabilities.
objection: AG2’s rebuttal is that even if AI improves accessibility, that benefit does not outweigh the broader harms it emphasized, including privacy, discrimination, educational degradation, and economic damage.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms across privacy, fairness, education, and the economy outweigh its benefits.
objection: AG2’s argument fails to consider AI’s potential to improve health outcomes, and any proper overall-welfare assessment must weigh those health benefits alongside the alleged harms.

target: AG1’s claim that health AI benefits justify AI overall because medical use can be done under normal confidentiality rules.
objection: Health-AI systems typically require processing sensitive medical or lifestyle data, so they still create substantial privacy harms; moreover, AI health recommendations can worsen outcomes for racial minorities, and those harms can offset the health benefits in an overall social-welfare judgment.

target: AG2’s claim that health AI inherently creates substantial privacy harm because it uses medical data.
objection: In routine clinical settings, health AI can be confined within existing confidentiality and informed-consent protections, using restricted-access clinical decision support rather than broad profiling, so it need not create substantial additional privacy harms.

target: AG1’s claim that clinical confidentiality and consent controls keep health-AI privacy harms minimal.
objection: Typical health-AI deployments often involve third-party vendor processing, logging, retraining, and other secondary uses outside the routine clinical care scope, so they bypass the confidentiality and consent protections that AG1 relies on.

target: AG2’s claim that health AI still causes substantial privacy harm despite security controls.
objection: Strong security and governance controls such as encryption, least-privilege access, and audit logging can materially reduce unauthorized access and misuse, so health AI does not typically have to generate substantial privacy harms.

target: AG2’s claim that health AI worsens racial-minority outcomes despite safeguards.
objection: Health-AI systems can be subgroup-validated and used with clinician oversight, which can detect and correct problematic disparities and prevent harm to racial minorities.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy, discrimination, and other harms are reduced enough that AI is good overall.
objection: Even with strong security controls, health AI can still cause substantial privacy harms through authorized sensitive inferences and downstream consequences such as discrimination, so the welfare impact is not reliably positive; discriminatory outcomes can also persist despite subgroup validation and oversight.

target: AG2’s claim that health-AI privacy harms remain a dominant negative even when patients have transparency and control.
objection: Health-AI deployments can provide granular notice, informed consent, opt-out, and meaningful recourse so patients can review and appeal how sensitive inferences are used, which substantially reduces the welfare harms from those inferences.

target: AG1’s claim that AI is not good overall only if health-AI privacy harms remain a major offset.
objection: Because privacy harms can still persist even when AI decisions are later appealed, and because discrimination risks remain despite oversight, the net welfare impact does not reliably turn positive just because some controls exist.

target: AG2’s claim that opaque AI decisions make privacy harms and racial-minority harms unchallengeable.
objection: Even when models are complex or proprietary, deployments can provide decision transparency, reason codes, user-facing explanations, and human appeal paths, which allow affected people to contest and verify the basis of AI-driven decisions.

target: AG1’s claim that appeal and human review make AI harms correctable.
objection: In real deployments, AI decisions often affect opportunities immediately, so later appeals may come too late to undo privacy losses or other harms; scheduled audits and monitoring also may miss harms between review cycles.

target: AG2’s claim that harms from AI-driven decisions are not reliably remediable through contestability or recourse.
objection: If AI decisions can be paused or reversed quickly through notice, explanation, and human review, then individuals can often get corrective outcomes in time; privacy harms from sensitive inferences can also be addressed by limiting downstream use of the challenged inference.

target: AG1’s claim that reversing an AI decision also remediates the privacy harm.
objection: Privacy harm often occurs as soon as a sensitive inference is generated and recorded, and that harm is not undone by later reversing the decision; the inference may also be reused in many downstream systems, so a single appeal cannot reliably stop all harmful uses.

target: AG1’s claim that contestability only needs to block the specific decision to fix privacy harms.
objection: Meaningful contestability would require reliable end-to-end data lineage from the inference to all downstream uses, but real AI deployments often lack such complete lineage because of proprietary pipelines and third-party integrations.

target: AG2’s claim that complete end-to-end data lineage is necessary for contestability to work.
objection: Contestability can be effective without perfect end-to-end lineage if organizations can identify the specific inference used in the decision and enforce governance that prevents further use of that inference within their own systems.

target: AG1’s claim that governance can be extended enough to control downstream uses and prevent privacy harms.
objection: In typical multi-vendor deployments, outputs and derived inferences flow through third-party and partner systems outside the deployer’s full control, so internal governance cannot reliably prevent all downstream uses of sensitive inferences.

target: AG2’s claim that cross-vendor privacy governance cannot work in practice.
objection: Deployers can use binding data-processing contracts, audit rights, technical enforcement at integration points, and privacy-preserving architectures such as data minimization and on-device or federated approaches, which can extend governance and reduce privacy exposure across vendors.

target: AG1’s claim that lineage/provenance and contractual controls can comprehensively manage inference-related data across vendors.
objection: In multi-vendor deployments, inference-related data often moves through proprietary systems and integrations, and contracts or audits generally cannot guarantee that every derivative signal will be excluded from retention and reuse across all vendors.

target: AG2’s claim that cross-vendor governance cannot reliably eliminate privacy exposure.
objection: AI data governance can maintain end-to-end lineage from model inputs through embeddings and logs, and with binding contracts plus technical policy enforcement, identified derivative data can be comprehensively prevented from being retained or reused; this means the weak assumption that there is no such evidence is false.

target: AG1’s claim that cross-vendor governance and privacy-preserving design make AI overall beneficial.
objection: Even with governance, proprietary vendor systems often prevent independent verification that all privacy-harming uses are blocked, so substantial privacy risks remain; moreover, such governance does not guarantee that discriminatory correlations will not be learned or that racial disparities will not re-emerge.
